newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks trapped in vicious circle on stock fall.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks trapped in vicious circle on stock fall.

text.p: Japan's mighty banking sector looks trapped in a vicious circle, as recent stock plunges have weakened the financial health of banks burdened by massive bad assets, igniting further share sales, traders say.
There are widespread worries that banks will be severely damaged financially by the stock market falls, which have trimmed unrealised profits on their share holdings.
"Given planned 'Big Bang' financial deregulation, investors have already turned critical eyes to the banks," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy general manager of Nomura Securities.

"It will be difficult for banks to move out of the current vicious circle in which falling stocks lead to falling latent profits on their stockholdings," Higashida said. "All we can do now is to wait for the market to regain some calmness."

Shares in leading Japanese banks have been heavily sold in recent days. On Thursday, they drove Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 average down 606.51 points, or 3.25 percent. The close of 18,073.87 was the market's weakest level for more than a year.
The Nikkei lost nearly 1,300 points in the first four trading days of this year.

Fierce sales by foreign brokerages knocked down shares of Sakura Bank Ltd, a major city bank, by their daily limit on Thursday. They ended 100 yen lower at 699 yen, while Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, another city bank, dropped to a 18-year low of below 200 yen, traders said.

Undermining bank shares is a widespread belief that lower overall stocks market prices will be a further setback to financial institutions already facing the difficult task of tackling mountains of bad loans.

Analysts estimate that if the Nikkei were to fall further to around 15,000, unrealised stock profits for most of Japanese banks would evaporate. Stock declines have already halved their unrealised stock profits to just below 8 trillion yen ($68.9 billion) from the end of September last year, the analysts said.
Goldman Sachs (Japan) said in recent commentary that the falling latent stock profits alone may not cause big worries for banks because they have other methods to raise funds.

"It is more important to see at what (Nikkei) level banks' appraisal losses on their securities' holdings get larger than their operating profits and force them to go into the red this fiscal year," it said.

For major banks, Goldman said in the report, the crucial level is 13,495, but for some others, it is much higher, like 16,842 for Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan, 16,751 for Nippon Credit Bank and 16,127 for Yasuda Trust & Banking Co Ltd.

Brokers said recent moves by cash-strapped Japanese companies to sell some of their bank and other shareholdings ahead of financial year-end book closings at the end of March were also undermining sentiment, brokers said.
"Bank share sales by foreign brokerages and the dissolving of cross-shareholdings hit the market hard," one broker said.

Brokers said Japan's traditional cross-shareholding system -- a practice by which companies hold each others' shares to strengthen business ties -- had lost its attraction in the face of planned Big Bang financial reforms.
Japan has drawn up a five-year Big Bang plan to liberalise its financial markets and to try to catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America.
Many agree the fate of stocks hinges on whether the government will take swift action to tackle structural reforms and get the economy back on a healthy recovery track.
Even so, few analysts believe the stock fall alone will rekindle the sort of major financial worries that would lead to panic selling by individuals.
